findings_addressed: FIX-1 / CODEX FINDING 1 [medium] — `sed|gsed|perl|ruby -i` parsed the edit PROGRAM as a path. WHAT CHANGED: the branch previously pushed EVERY non-flag token through consider(), so the script/expression argument — which is prose, not a path — was tested as a write target and an allowed write was denied for merely mentioning a protected segment. Replaced with an explicit operand rule, written into the header comment directly above the code it describes so the two cannot drift: (1) a token starting with `-` is a flag, never a target; (2) a short cluster containing `e`/`E`/`f` supplies the program — GLUED when characters follow that letter (`-e'EXPR'`, `-pe'EXPR'`), otherwise the NEXT non-flag token is the program (`-e EXPR`, `-pe EXPR`, `-f script.sed`) — and either way the program is consumed, never considered; (3) `--expression`/`--file`, with or without `=`, do the same; (4) if no flag supplied a program, the FIRST bare operand IS the program (`sed -i 's/a/b/' FILE...`) and is skipped; (5) every remaining bare operand is a file and IS considered. In-place detection was also moved so it walks FLAG tokens only — previously a program argument could itself be mistaken for `-i`. ARMS THAT NOW COVER IT: 44, 45, 46 (the review's three named cases, all ALLOW), 47, 48, 49, 50 (the four that were actually RED), with 51/51b/51c/51d/51e/52 as the paired true-positives proving the false-positive fix did not open a false negative.

FIX-1 / FINDING 1 — THE REVIEWER'S WITNESS DOES NOT REPRODUCE, BUT THE MECHANISM IS REAL. Stated plainly because a fix should not silently paper over a wrong witness. The review's literal command, `sed -i 's#src/rust/lib.rs#x#' dev/plans/note.md`, was measured against the pre-fix hook at d31430ce and it ALLOWED, exactly as desired. The reason is the `#` delimiters: normalize_path splits on `/`, so that token yields the segments `s#src` | `rust` | `lib.rs#x#`, and `s#src` is not `src`. The reviewer's diagnosis of the CODE was nonetheless correct — the expression really was being sent through consider() — so the defect class is genuine and only the demonstration was off. The reproducing witnesses, each OBSERVED RED before the fix, are the ones where the expression's own tokens normalize onto a protected segment: `sed -i 's/src/lib/' dev/plans/note.md` (arm 47, denied on segment `src`), `sed -i -e 's/tests/checks/' dev/plans/note.md` (arm 48, segment `tests`), `perl -i -pe 's/engine/motor/' dev/plans/note.md` (arm 49, segment `engine`), and `sed -i 's,^,# see src/rust/lib.rs,' dev/plans/note.md` (arm 50). Arm 44 is kept in the suite anyway, as the ALLOW it is, because it is the case the review names and a future reader will look for it.

FIX-1 / FINDING 1, SECOND LAYER FOUND WHILE FIXING — the quoted program word is SHREDDED by the tokenizer. Arm 50 stayed red after the operand rule landed. Cause: `read -ra` splits on whitespace with no notion of quoting, so the single shell word `'s,^,# see src/rust/lib.rs,'` arrives as three tokens; rule 4 skipped only the first, and the middle shard `src/rust/lib.rs,'` was then read as a file operand and denied. Added absorb_quoted_word(), called at every point a token is identified as the program: it walks the index past the rest of a word whose quote the token did not close, honouring backslash escapes OUTSIDE single quotes so the `'a'\''b'` idiom balances correctly. It relies on bash's dynamic scoping to advance scan_simple_command's loop index, is bounded by the token count so it cannot loop, and over-absorbs at worst — the fail-open direction, consistent with the rest of the hook. NON-VACUITY OF ITS OWN ARMS, verified rather than asserted: arms 50b (`sed -i 's/it'\''s/x/' src/rust/lib.rs`) and 50c (`sed -i "s/don't/do not/" src/rust/lib.rs`) both go RED when absorb_quoted_word is deliberately altered to swallow to end of line, which is exactly the over-absorption they exist to catch. The sabotage was applied to a copy-restored file and reverted; `grep -n 'q="x"'` on the committed hook returns nothing.

FIX-1 / CODEX FINDING 2 [low] — glued `>|FILE` clobber redirection slipped, AND IT WAS WIDER THAN REPORTED. The review says the code caught the spaced `>| FILE` and missed only the glued form. Measured against the pre-fix hook, seat=orchestrator: BOTH slipped. `printf x >|src/rust/lib.rs` -> no decision, and `printf x >| src/rust/lib.rs` -> no decision, where deny was expected in each case. The cause explains why the spaced form failed too and why the token-level `\>\|` alternation could never have worked: scan_bash_command rewrites every `|` to a newline BEFORE tokenizing, so `>|` was torn in half and the target landed alone on the following line as a bare word with no operator in front of it. WHAT CHANGED: fixed at the source rather than at the matcher — `stripped="${stripped//>|/>}"` folds `>|` to `>` immediately after heredoc stripping and before the `||`/`|` splits. The fold is lossless for scanning: `>|` is a single unambiguous bash operator and `>` is the same redirection for target-extraction purposes, and in valid shell a `>|` can never be half of a `||`. The now-unreachable `\>\|` alternation in the token regex was REMOVED rather than left as dead code claiming a capability it no longer provides. ARMS THAT NOW COVER IT: 53 (glued, was RED), 54 (spaced, was RED — contra the review), 54b (`2>|`, fd-numbered, was RED), 55 (glued into dev/plans/** must still ALLOW, so the fix cannot over-block), 55b (a read-only `grep -n '>|' ...` must stay silent, so the rewrite cannot turn a quoted MENTION of the operator into a redirection).

FIX-1 / FINDING 2 — THE COMMENT/CODE RECONCILIATION THE ORCHESTRATOR REQUIRED. Finding 2 was at root a DRIFT defect: the header claimed `>|` coverage the code did not implement. So every form the comment claims is now asserted by an arm rather than believed, and the comment was rewritten to point at those arms by number. Result of auditing the whole matcher: `>` `>>` `1>` `2>>` in both spaced and glued shape all worked as documented (now pinned by arms 6, 10, 56a-56d). TWO FURTHER MISMATCHES WERE FOUND, and BOTH were resolved toward the CODE, because in both cases the code was right and the comment was merely silent or wrong. (a) `&>` and `&>>` WORK — the `&` split leaves `>FILE`/`>>FILE`, which the glued branch catches — but the comment never claimed them. Resolved by DOCUMENTING them and adding arms 56e/56f. (b) `>>|` and `&>|`: I first wrote the comment to say these are 'not covered'. That was itself wrong, because the `>|`->`>` fold makes them deny incidentally. Rather than leave a fresh mismatch, I measured them — `bash -n -c 'printf x >>| /dev/null'` and the `&>|` equivalent are both SYNTAX ERRORS, while `>|` and `2>|` parse fine — and the comment now records exactly that: no write can occur through either form, so nothing needs guarding, and the incidental deny is a harmless over-block on a command that could never run. No arm claims `>>|`/`&>|` coverage.

DESIGN FINDING THE STEWARD ASKED FOR — CAN THE HOOK DETERMINE WHICH AGENT/SEAT IS INVOKING IT? The honest answer is QUALIFIED YES-AND-NO, and the 'no' half is the important one. YES for a SPAWNED subagent: the PreToolUse payload carries `agent_type` (e.g. "orchestrator") alongside `agent_id`, so a spawned orchestrator/steward is positively identifiable with no cooperation from the agent and no configuration. NO for a MAIN-THREAD session: per the Claude Code v2.1.220 binary's own field documentation, `agent_id` is "Absent for the main thread, even in --agent sessions", and `agent_type` is present on the main thread ONLY for a session started with `--agent`. A `/orchestrate` or `/steward` session is an ORDINARY session running a slash command — no `--agent` flag — so its top-level thread carries NEITHER field. From the payload alone such a session is byte-for-byte indistinguishable from any other session in this repo, including a human's ad-hoc one. There is no way to close that gap from inside a hook: the information simply is not sent. CONSEQUENCE FOR THE SEAT MODEL: the hook mechanically guards the spawned case and can only OPT-IN guard the main-thread case, via the $FATHOMDB_SEAT environment variable set at session LAUNCH. Since dev/design/orchestration.md § 1.1 establishes that 'main thread' is role-indexed and that a /steward session's top-level thread IS the Steward, the usual Steward seat is exactly the unguarded case unless the launcher sets the env var. That is a real hole in the guard, not a rounding error, and it is stated in the hook header rather than papered over.

SECONDARY FINDING — WHY $FATHOMDB_SEAT OUTRANKING THE PAYLOAD IS NOT AN EVASION HATCH. The resolution order is env, then agent_type, then UNKNOWN. It has to be env-first or a main-thread seat could never opt in. That ordering is safe because an agent cannot set the variable for its own hook invocations: each Bash tool call is a separate process, `export` does not persist between them, and the hook is spawned by the harness with the SESSION's environment, not by the agent's shell. The env var is therefore a launcher-side control, not an agent-side one. Documented in the hook header and covered by test arms 38 and 39 (precedence proven in both directions).

Created .claude/hooks/seat-path-guard.sh — a PreToolUse hook implementing the dev/design/orchestration.md § 1.2 write-path boundary. Guarded seats: orchestrator, steward (matched case-insensitively, whitespace-trimmed). Denied: any path with a `src`, `engine`, or `tests` SEGMENT, plus test-source basenames (test_*.{py,sh,rs,ts,js}, *_test.{py,sh,rs,go,ts,js}, *.test.{ts,tsx,js,mjs}, *.spec.{ts,tsx,js,mjs}, conftest.py). Matching is segment-based on the NORMALIZED target (`.`/`..` resolved, surrounding quotes stripped), so it is identical for absolute paths, repo-relative paths, and paths inside ANY worktree — a guarded seat must not write source anywhere, not only under $CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR.

DENY-LIST, NOT ALLOW-LIST — a design choice worth the reviewer's eye. The hook objects ONLY to § 1.2's MUST-NEVER column and stays silent about everything else. It does not verify that a write falls INSIDE the MAY column. Reason: an allow-list would deny a coordinating seat editing README.md, .github/workflows/*, Cargo.toml or any of the dozens of paths § 1.2 never enumerated, and an over-blocking guard gets switched off, which is strictly worse than no guard. Consequence to be aware of: the hook enforces the never-list, not the full boundary.

PRECEDENCE RULE, stated in the header and covered by arm 14 + its allow-twin 14b: scripts/tests/** is BOTH under the allowed scripts/** and a test source. TEST SOURCE WINS — it is DENIED. Rationale: the MUST-NEVER column is the invariant and the MAY column is the convenience, so on collision the invariant governs. Structurally guaranteed, not merely intended: the basename test runs BEFORE the segment walk in protected_reason().

FAIL-OPEN IS STRUCTURAL, NOT PROMISED. `trap 'exit 0' EXIT` plus the DELIBERATE absence of `set -e`/`set -u` (a documented departure from the repo's `set -euo pipefail` convention, which is right for gates and wrong for a project-global hook) makes a non-zero exit unreachable. Safe because the deny signal travels in stdout JSON, never in the exit code. Every degraded path allows: malformed JSON, empty stdin, valid JSON of the wrong shape, no jq, no jq AND no python3, no base64 decoder, payload over 200 KB, unknown seat, unknown tool. Test arm 4-of-the-shape-block asserts the trap is present so the posture cannot silently regress.

SILENCE ON ALLOW is part of the contract and is asserted (arms 42, 43): an allowed call gets NO stdout and NO stderr — not `permissionDecision: allow`, because emitting allow would auto-approve the call and bypass the human's permission prompt for something the guard has no opinion on. stderr silence needed an actual fix: bash itself warns 'ignored null byte in input' from the command substitution that reads the payload, so the read is wrapped in `{ ... } 2>/dev/null`. Found by probing with binary stdin, not by reading the code.

BASH IS THE LOAD-BEARING SURFACE and is covered accordingly. Measured evidence from the brief: the two observed orchestrator sessions made 76 and 193 Bash calls and ZERO Edit/Write calls, so an Edit/Write-only guard would have inspected 0% of the actual write path. The scanner detects: redirections `>` `>>` `>|` `1>` `2>>` and the glued `>FILE` form; heredocs (via the introducing line's redirect); `tee [-a]`; `sed -i` / `perl -i` (any `-*i*` flag); `cp` / `mv` / `install` / `rsync` / `ln` destinations (last non-flag operand); `dd of=`; `rm` / `shred` / `unlink` / `touch` / `truncate` / `mkfifo`; `git checkout|restore|apply|mv|rm|stash|clean`; and inline `python3 -c` / `node -e` / `ruby -e` / `perl -e` bodies that carry a write indicator (open() with a w/a/x mode, write_text, writeFileSync, appendFileSync, createWriteStream, os.replace/rename, shutil.copy/move).

HEREDOC BODIES ARE STRIPPED BEFORE SCANNING (arm 34). A body is data, not shell: markdown blockquotes and pasted shell examples routinely contain `>` and `src/...`, so scanning bodies would deny at random. The heredoc's own redirect stays on the introducing line and is still caught (arm 3).

FALSE-POSITIVE GUARDS ARE FIRST-CLASS ARMS, not an afterthought: `grep foo src/x.rs` (arm 11), `cat src/x.rs` (30), `git log src/` (31), `git diff src/... > dev/plans/...` — read a protected path while writing an allowed one (32), read-only inspection across `&&` (33), heredoc body mentioning src (34), unhandled tool Read (35). A guard that blocks reads gets turned off within a day.

RED-FIRST DISCIPLINE — RED WAS OBSERVED TWICE, and the second observation is the one that matters. (1) HOOK ABSENT: `bash <hook>` rc=127, empty stdout; 3 PASS / 51 FAIL — every behavioural arm red, but for the uninteresting reason that nothing ran. (2) HOOK = FAIL-OPEN STUB (`#!/usr/bin/env bash` + `trap 'exit 0' EXIT` + `cat >/dev/null` + `exit 0`): 29 PASS / 25 FAIL, and the 25 failures were EXACTLY the DENY arms (1, 2, 3, 9, 10, 13, 14, 15/15b/15c, 17-27, 29, 39, 40, 41), with every ALLOW/fail-open/shape arm green. That is the non-vacuity witness this suite needed: the hook's contract is 'stay silent unless sure', which `true` satisfies trivially, so ONLY the deny arms discriminate a working guard from a no-op — and they were all proven capable of going red before the hook existed. The stub was never committed; it was written to .claude/hooks/ (gitignored at that moment) and deleted before the implementation was written.

blockers_encountered.description: BLOCKER THE BRIEF DID NOT ANTICIPATE — .claude/hooks/ IS GITIGNORED. The brief directs the hook to `.claude/hooks/seat-path-guard.sh`, 'same home as the existing .claude/hooks/git-commit-check.sh'. But .gitignore lines 16-19 read `.claude/*` with only `!.claude/agents/` and `!.claude/commands/` un-ignored, so .claude/hooks/ is ignored wholesale and does not exist in a linked worktree or a fresh clone at all (the three hooks in the primary checkout are untracked local files). A file written there is INVISIBLE TO GIT: it cannot be committed without -f, cannot be cherry-picked to mainline, would not appear in the reviewer's diff, and would be absent in CI — where the newly-registered test suite would then hard-fail looking for it. The slice would have delivered nothing.
blockers_encountered.resolution: Added the SMALLEST possible negation to .gitignore, immediately after the existing `!.claude/commands/` line, un-ignoring EXACTLY ONE file: `!.claude/hooks/` then `.claude/hooks/*` then `!.claude/hooks/seat-path-guard.sh`. Verified with `git add .claude/hooks/` that the ONLY staged path is .claude/hooks/seat-path-guard.sh — git-commit-check.sh, session-start.sh and session-stop.sh stay ignored and untracked exactly as before. This matches the stated intent of the ignore block's own comment ('.claude/ holds SHARED harness tooling (tracked) alongside per-user/local files (ignored)'): the guard is shared, reviewed, CI-run tooling; the other three are per-user. .gitignore is not on the DO-NOT-TOUCH list, and a .gitignore change in a linked worktree has ZERO effect on any other worktree or on the live orchestrator until it is cherry-picked. FLAGGED FOR THE REVIEWER/ORCHESTRATOR: if you prefer, the alternative is to move the hook under the tracked scripts/ tree (e.g. scripts/hooks/seat-path-guard.sh) and drop the .gitignore hunk — the hook itself is path-agnostic and only the test's HOOK= line and the future settings.json wiring would move. I did NOT take that route because it deviates from the path the brief names.

blockers_encountered.description: ARM 16 (the Phase-1 UNWIRED marker) had a vacuity trap of its own: .claude/settings.json is gitignored and per-user, so it is ABSENT from this linked worktree, from a fresh clone, and from CI. A bare `grep -L seat-path-guard .claude/settings.json` would have passed for the wrong reason — 'the file isn't there' rather than 'the hook isn't wired' — which is exactly the shape of failure the arm exists to prevent.
blockers_encountered.resolution: Three-part construction. (a) The detector is proven against a POSITIVE fixture first: a synthetic settings.json that DOES wire the hook must be detected, or the arm fails. (b) Candidate settings files are resolved from every place one can really live: $REPO_ROOT/.claude/, the PRIMARY CHECKOUT's .claude/ (reached via `git rev-parse --git-common-dir` + dirname, since a linked worktree has none of its own), and $CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR/.claude/ — settings.json and settings.local.json in each, deduplicated. (c) The proven detector is applied to each file that exists. In this worktree it really did reach and check /home/coreyt/projects/fathomdb/.claude/settings.json and settings.local.json, and both are clean. If NO settings file exists anywhere (fresh clone / CI) the arm passes with an explicit loud message saying the invariant holds vacuously and pointing at the proven detector, so the pass is never mistaken for a positive observation.

additional_changes_made_in_scope: EVASION PATHS THE BASH DETECTION DOES NOT COVER — recorded here because the brief asked for them explicitly, and stated just as prominently in the script header under 'LIMITATIONS — READ BEFORE TRUSTING'. Bash guarding is BEST-EFFORT, NOT A SANDBOX; it raises the cost of an ACCIDENTAL violation and does not stop a determined one. Known unclosed evasions: (1) variable indirection — `D=src; printf x > "$D/lib.rs"`; (2) decoded or constructed commands — `base64 -d <<<... | sh`, `eval "$(...)"`; (3) command substitution in the target — `printf x > "$(printf src/lib.rs)"`; (4) writing through a helper — ./my-writer.sh, make, a cargo build script, any program the hook sees only by name; (5) `git apply` / `patch` — the PATCH BODY is never inspected, so a diff touching src/** passes unless a protected path appears in argv; (6) quoted paths containing spaces are tokenized naively (`read -ra` on whitespace), so `> "src/my file.rs"` yields the token `"src/my` which still normalizes to a `src` segment and denies, but the reverse case — an allowed path containing a space — could mis-split; (7) `;` `|` `&&` INSIDE a quoted string split the command incorrectly (the splitter is textual, not a shell parser), which can both over- and under-block; (8) MultiEdit and NotebookEdit are NOT covered — only Edit, Write and Bash, per the brief's explicit three-tool scope. (8) is a named Phase-2 gap rather than a silent scope change; MultiEdit in particular carries file_path and would be a one-line addition if the reviewer wants it now.

ACCEPTED OVER-BLOCK, documented in the header: because segment matching runs over the WHOLE normalized path, a path whose ancestor directory is literally named src/engine/tests OUTSIDE this repo (the common `~/src/notes.md` shape) is denied for a guarded seat. Deliberate: guarded seats work inside the repo, over-blocking is the safe direction for a guard whose purpose is stopping source writes, and the deny reason names the path so a human can see instantly what happened. The alternative (anchoring to $CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR) would have broken the brief's requirement that the guard work for paths inside ANY worktree.

NOTE ON `engine/**`, following the observation ASH-A already recorded in its own output.json: `engine/**` is a CONCEPTUAL path — the engine crate physically lives at src/rust/crates/fathomdb-engine and is therefore already covered by the `src` segment rule. The hook implements a literal `engine` segment anyway, so both the conceptual and any future real engine/ tree are covered. Arms 10, 19 and 21 use literal engine/ paths.
